S E C T I O N 1 · A S H A R P E R R I S K
Stranded Assets: When Value Simply Disappears
The risk that is hardest for traditional financial models to see coming.
The Definition An asset that suffers unanticipated or premature write-downs, devaluations, or conversion to liabilities —
before the end of its expected economic life.
The Classic Example Fossil fuel reserves currently on company balance sheets may never be extractable if climate policy tightens fast 
enough — reserves priced as assets today, worthless tomorrow.
Why It's Different From Other Risks Stranded asset risk isn't about an accident or a scandal — it is the market itself re-pricing an entire asset class as 
the energy transition accelerates.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 09

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
Which category of sustainability risk best describes fossil fuel 
reserves that may become unextractable due to future climate policy?
A Reputational risk
B Litigation risk
C Stranded asset risk
D Physical risk
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. Stranded asset risk
Stranded asset risk specifically refers to assets that 
lose most of their expected value before the end of 
their useful economic life — exactly the situation 
facing fossil fuel reserves as climate policy and the 
energy transition accelerate.

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
The Opportunity Landscape
Where sustainability stops being a defensive cost and becomes an actual source of competitive advantage.
11

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E T A X O N O M Y
Five Categories of Sustainability Opportunity
The flip side of the risk landscape — where genuine value gets created, not just protected.
Eco-Efficiency
Cutting energy, water, and 
material costs directly through 
better resource use — savings 
that hit the bottom line 
immediately.
Innovation & New 
Markets
Sustainability constraints often 
force genuinely new products, 
services, and business models 
into existence.
Brand & Customer 
Loyalty
A credible sustainability record 
increasingly shapes purchasing 
decisions, especially among 
younger consumers.
Access to Capital
Green finance and ESG-driven 
investment flows can 
materially lower the cost of 
raising capital.
Talent Attraction
Purpose-driven employer 
branding is now a real factor in 
recruiting and retaining skilled 
employees.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 12

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E F O U N D A T I O N A L A R G U M E N T
Porter's Hypothesis: Regulation Can Drive Innovation
A genuinely counterintuitive claim from one of the most cited strategists in business history.
The Conventional View Environmental regulation is a cost that makes firms less competitive — compliance diverts resources away from 
productive investment.
Porter's Counter-Argument (Porter & van der 
Linde, 1995)
Well-designed regulation can trigger innovation that partially or fully offsets its own compliance cost — an 
"innovation offset."
The Mechanism Regulation forces firms to notice resource inefficiencies they had been ignoring — cutting waste, energy, and 
materials is very often also cutting cost.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 13

S E C T I O N 2 · B U I L D I N G O N T H E H Y P O T H E S I S
Creating Shared Value (Porter & Kramer, 2011)
A framework for finding competitive advantage inside social and environmental problems, not despite them.
Reconceiving Products & Markets Designing products and services that address unmet social needs — turning underserved populations into new 
markets.
Redefining Productivity in the Value Chain Rethinking energy use, logistics, sourcing, and labor practices as productivity levers, not just cost centers.
Building Supportive Industry Clusters Investing in the local suppliers, infrastructure, and skills a company's own success actually depends on.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 14

S E C T I O N 2 · A C R I T I C A L L O O K
Shared Value Has Its Critics Too
Not every scholar accepted "Creating Shared Value" as the breakthrough Porter and Kramer claimed — the critique matters as much as the framework.
Not Entirely New
Critics (Crane et al., 2014) noted the concept closely echoed earlier work — Elkington's 
Triple Bottom Line, Prahalad and Hart's "base of the pyramid" thinking — without fully 
crediting it.
Ignores Real Trade-offs
The "win-win" framing can understate genuine tensions between profit and social good —
not every social problem has a profitable solution waiting inside it.
A Shallow View of Responsibility
Focusing only on where social good and profit overlap can let companies ignore harms that 
fall outside that overlap entirely.
Still Widely Used, With Eyes Open
The framework remains genuinely useful for finding strategic opportunity — as long as it 
isn't mistaken for the whole of a company's ethical responsibility.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 15

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When Opportunity Was Seized Early: Ørsted
From "DONG Energy" to the World's Leading Offshore Wind Developer
A majority Danish state-owned oil and gas company made a deliberate strategic bet in the late 2000s to pivot toward offshore wind — divesting its oil and gas 
business and rebranding as Ørsted in 2017.
The Risk They Avoided
By exiting fossil fuels well ahead of the market, Ørsted sidestepped much of the stranded￾asset exposure now facing slower-moving oil and gas majors.
The Opportunity They Captured
Early, sustained investment in offshore wind technology built engineering expertise and 
project experience competitors could not quickly replicate.
The Market Outcome
Ørsted became widely recognized as one of the world's leading offshore wind developers, 
turning a former fossil fuel utility into a renewable energy leader.
The Lesson
The company didn't just reduce its risk profile — it converted an anticipated regulatory and 
market shift into a durable competitive advantage.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 16

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
What did Porter and van der Linde (1995) argue well-designed 
environmental regulation could trigger?
A Guaranteed bankruptcy for regulated firms
B An "innovation offset" that can partially or fully offset compliance costs
C A permanent reduction in industry profitability
D No effect on firm behavior whatsoever
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. An "innovation offset" that can partially 
or fully offset compliance costs
Porter and van der Linde argued that well-designed 
regulation forces firms to notice inefficiencies they 
had been ignoring, triggering innovation that can 
partially or fully offset the cost of compliance — the 
foundational argument behind treating sustainability 
as a competitive opportunity.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 18

S E C T I O N 3 O F 4
Stakeholder Theory & Engagement
Who a company actually owes value to — and the frameworks for deciding what matters most.
19

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E F O U N D A T I O N A L D E B A T E
Shareholder Primacy vs. Stakeholder Theory
Shareholder Primacy 
(Friedman, 1970)
Stakeholder Theory (Freeman, 
1984)
"The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits" — famously 
argued in Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times essay.
A business exists to create value for all groups with a stake in it — not 
shareholders alone (Freeman, "Strategic Management: A Stakeholder 
Approach").
Managers are agents of shareholders; other obligations should be handled 
through law and market forces, not managerial discretion.
Customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and shareholders are all 
legitimate stakeholders whose interests deserve consideration.
Simple, singular objective function: maximize shareholder returns within the 
law.
Requires balancing multiple, sometimes competing interests — genuinely 
harder to execute, and to measure.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 20

S E C T I O N 3 · A M O D E R N T U R N I N G P O I N T
The Business Roundtable Statement (2019)
181 CEOs of America's largest companies publicly broke with over two decades of stated shareholder primacy.
"We commit to a fundamental commitment to all of our stakeholders — customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and shareholders." — Business 
Roundtable, August 19, 2019
What Changed
Every Business Roundtable governance statement since 
1997 had endorsed shareholder primacy — this 
reversed that stance explicitly.
The Critical Follow-Up
A widely cited study (Bebchuk & Tallarita, 2020–22) 
found most signatory companies made no changes to 
governance documents or executive pay structures 
afterward.
The "PR Hypothesis" vs. "Commitment 
Hypothesis"
Researchers frame this as an open empirical question: 
was the statement a genuine shift, or mainly a public￾relations gesture?
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 21

S E C T I O N 3 · D E C I D I N G W H O M A T T E R S M O S T
The Stakeholder Salience Model
Not every stakeholder can be prioritized equally — this model gives managers a structured way to decide.
Power Does this stakeholder have the ability to actually influence the organization — through markets, regulation, or 
public pressure?
Legitimacy Is this stakeholder's claim on the organization socially or legally recognized as appropriate?
Urgency How time-sensitive or critical is this stakeholder's claim right now?
The Framework (Mitchell, Agle & Wood, 1997) Stakeholders holding all three attributes ("definitive stakeholders") demand the most immediate management 
attention — a practical triage tool.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 22

S E C T I O N 3 · T U R N I N G T H E O R Y I N T O P R A C T I C E
Materiality Assessment
How a company actually decides which sustainability issues deserve its limited attention and resources.
The Core Question Which issues are both significant to the business's financial performance and significant to its stakeholders —
and where do the two overlap most?
The Materiality Matrix A common visual tool plots issues on two axes — importance to stakeholders, and importance to business 
success — surfacing the handful that matter most.
Why It Matters Here This is the practical bridge between stakeholder theory and corporate strategy — it turns "consider all 
stakeholders" into an actual, prioritized action list.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 23

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
"Using the Stakeholder Salience Model, who

Consider power, legitimacy, and urgency together, not just one.

THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 24

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
In the Stakeholder Salience Model (Mitchell, Agle & Wood, 1997), 
what three attributes determine a stakeholder's priority?
A Size, revenue, and location
B Power, legitimacy, and urgency
C Age, gender, and income
D Loyalty, tenure, and satisfaction
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Power, legitimacy, and urgency
The Stakeholder Salience Model ranks stakeholders by 
power (ability to influence), legitimacy (socially/legally 
recognized claim), and urgency (time-sensitivity of the 
claim) — those holding all three are classified as 
"definitive" stakeholders demanding the most 
attention.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 25

S E C T I O N 4 O F 4
Long-Term Value Creation
How everything covered today ultimately shows up in the actual price of capital.
26

S E C T I O N 4 · T H E C A P I T A L M A R K E T S S H I F T
ESG Investing & Access to Capital
Sustainability performance increasingly determines not just reputation, but the actual cost of a company's money.
The Growth of ESG Investing Environmental, Social, and Governance criteria are now a standard input for a large and growing share of global 
institutional investment decisions.
Why Investors Care ESG performance is used as a proxy for management quality and long-term risk exposure — not (primarily) as an 
ethical statement by the investor.
The Practical Effect Strong sustainability performers increasingly find it easier, and sometimes cheaper, to raise both debt and equity 
capital than weaker performers in the same industry.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 27

S E C T I O N 4 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
How Sustainability Risk Prices Into the Cost of Capital
G I V E N
Two companies each raise ₹100 crore via a 10-year corporate bond
Company A (strong ESG rating): investors demand a 4.5% interest rate
Company B (weak ESG rating, higher perceived climate/governance risk): 
investors demand 5.2%
F O R M U L A
Annual Interest Cost = Principal × Interest Rate
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Company A: ₹100 crore × 4.5% = ₹4.5 crore per year
2 Company B: ₹100 crore × 5.2% = ₹5.2 crore per year
3 Extra annual cost for Company B: ₹0.7 crore — roughly ₹7 crore over the life of the bond, purely from the market's perception of risk.
₹7 Cr Extra Cost A weaker sustainability risk profile alone can cost a company crores over the life of a single bond — this is what "sustainability 
affects the cost of capital" means in practice.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 28

S E C T I O N 4 · M E A S U R I N G R E A L P R O G R E S S
Reporting Frameworks That Signal Long-Term Value
Investors and regulators increasingly expect structured, comparable sustainability disclosure — not a one-off marketing document.
GRI Standards
The most widely used global framework 
for sustainability reporting across 
environmental, social, and economic 
impact.
India's BRSR
SEBI's mandatory Business Responsibility 
and Sustainability Reporting for India's 
top 1,000 listed companies.
Integrated Reporting
Combines financial and sustainability 
performance into a single report, 
showing how they actually connect —
not two separate documents.
Science Based Targets (SBTi)
Independently verifies that a company's 
emissions targets are actually consistent 
with the Paris Agreement's temperature 
goals.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 29

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
In the cost-of-capital example, why did Company B pay a higher 
interest rate than Company A?
A Company B borrowed a larger amount of money
B Investors priced in greater perceived climate and governance risk
C Company B had a shorter loan term
D Interest rates are unrelated to a company's sustainability profile
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Investors priced in greater perceived 
climate and governance risk
Investors price bonds based on perceived risk. A 
weaker ESG rating signals greater exposure to 
regulatory, physical, and governance risk — so 
investors demand a higher interest rate to 
compensate for that additional risk, directly raising the 
company's cost of capital.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 30

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
The Business Case, End to End
Four ideas, one continuous argument — from what can go wrong, to what a company is worth because of how it responds.
The Risk Landscape Names the downside: regulatory, physical, reputational, litigation, and stranded-asset risk — real, costed, and no longer avoidable.
The Opportunity Landscape Reframes the same terrain as competitive advantage — eco-efficiency, innovation, brand, capital, and talent.
Stakeholder Theory & 
Engagement Supplies the "who": which stakeholders a company must actually satisfy, and how to prioritize among them.
Long-Term Value Creation Shows where it all lands — in the market's own pricing of a company's capital, today.
THE BUSINESS CASE FOR SUSTAINABILITY 31

◆ INTERACTIVE A P P L Y I T A L L
"Pick one real company you know well. Where 
does it sit on the risk landscape, the opportunity 
landscape — and which stakeholder is it currently 
underweighting?"
This is the exact exercise a sustainability strategy team runs in practice.
